pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Rock layers and Earth's history (reading cross-sections & strata)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS2 Science working scientifically — interpret diagrams; upper-KS2 Rocks/Earth):** Pupils read and label cross-section diagrams of Earth's interior and of rock strata, and interpret which layers formed first.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 4-ESS1-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS1-1] (principle of superposition).

- **Operational details:** This is a REPRESENTATIONAL node: the skill is reading geological diagrams, not memorising facts. Three sub-skills: (1) label Earth's interior on a cross-section — crust, mantle, outer core, inner core; (2) read a sedimentary strata diagram and apply SUPERPOSITION — undisturbed layers are laid down bottom-first, so the deepest layer is oldest and the top is youngest; (3) trace a pathway on a rock-cycle diagram. The load-bearing insight is superposition and the idea that a cross-section is a slice through time — reading UP the layers is reading FORWARD through Earth's history. Teach by having children build up layers themselves (deposit sediment over 'time') then read the finished stack, so the diagram is understood as a record of events in order, not a static picture.
bestPractices: Distinguish the two diagram types explicitly: Earth's interior (crust→core, a spatial cross-section) vs sedimentary strata (a time record) — children conflate them.
Teach superposition by DEPOSITING layers in sequence, then reading the stack: bottom = first/oldest, top = last/youngest.
Frame a strata cross-section as a slice through time — reading up the layers reads forward through history.
Rehearse diagram literacy both ways: label a blank diagram, and narrate the story a labelled diagram tells.
Use fossils within layers as datable markers to reinforce that deeper fossils are older.
keyRepresentations: A labelled Earth-interior cross-section (crust, mantle, outer core, inner core).
A sedimentary strata column with layers to order oldest→youngest (superposition).
A rock-cycle diagram with traceable pathways (igneous↔sedimentary↔metamorphic).
A 'slice through time' annotated strata diagram linking depth to age.
Fossil markers embedded in layers as relative-dating clues.
commonMisconceptions: 'The top layer is oldest' — reversing superposition.
Confusing Earth's interior layers (crust/mantle/core) with sedimentary strata — two different kinds of 'layers'.
'A cross-section shows what's on the surface' — not reading it as a cut-through view.
'Rock layers formed all at once' — missing that each stratum records a separate episode over long time.
'The rock cycle has a fixed one-way order' — not seeing it as a network of reversible pathways.
'Deeper always means the mantle/core' — conflating shallow sedimentary depth with planetary-scale depth.

learn.summary: For 10–11 year-olds, teach reading of geological diagrams (not fact memorisation): label Earth's interior cross-section (crust, mantle, outer core, inner core); apply superposition to sedimentary strata (deepest = oldest, top = youngest); and trace pathways on a rock-cycle diagram. The load-bearing insight is that an undisturbed strata cross-section is a slice through time — reading up the layers reads forward through Earth's history. A route recommended by the source pedagogy is to have children build strata themselves (deposit sediment episode by episode over 'millions of years', embed fossils), then read the finished stack as a record of events in order; this is a proposed approach rather than a format proven superior to others. Keep the two diagram types distinct: Earth's interior is a spatial cross-section, while strata are a time record.

activities.title: Build strata over time, then read the finished column
feedback: If a learner names the top layer as oldest ('it's at the top, so it came first / it's been there longest'), demonstrate directly: drop coloured sand into a clear jar layer by layer so each new layer visibly buries the older ones beneath — the first sand poured ends up at the bottom.

If a learner draws the next new layer at the bottom or inserts it between existing layers, point out that new sediment settles on the current top surface; that is where the newest layer forms, so draw it on top of the stack.

When a learner points to the bottom layer and explains lower layers were deposited before the ones above, confirm this is superposition and ask them to read the whole stack in age order oldest→youngest.
activities.rationale: Superposition is a temporal idea, so building the sequence over time and then reading the result lets 'deepest = oldest' follow from what the learner directly observed, making diagram reading an act of construction as well as recognition. A live deposition sequence with era labels and embedded fossils lets learners use the fossils in each layer as evidence of what happened when, making the time-record interpretation concrete.
sourceClaims: Principle of superposition: in undisturbed sedimentary sequences the oldest layer is at the bottom and the youngest at the top; cross-sections record events in order.
learnerActions: Deposit layers in sequence across 'millions of years': lay a sandy beach layer, then a layer of volcanic ash, then a muddy seabed on top, giving each layer an era label.
Drop an early marker fossil (e.g. a trilobite) into one of the first layers and a clearly later fossil (e.g. a dinosaur bone) into a layer added later.
Stop depositing and switch to reading the finished cross-section: point to the layer that was laid down first and the one laid down last.
State and justify the rule: the deepest layer is oldest and the top is youngest, because each new layer settled on top of the ones already there.
Predict: if a river dumped new mud here next year, where would the new layer form, and would it be the oldest or youngest?
activities.intendedInsight: An undisturbed strata cross-section is a record of events in order: because you watched the bottom layer arrive first, deepest = oldest and reading up the cliff reads forward through time. In this undisturbed stack, the deeper a fossil lies, the older it is.

activities.title: Read then draw: separate labelling from reading the order
feedback: A learner who reads the top layer as first-deposited because it is 'what you see first' should revisit the deposition demo: the earliest material is buried deepest.
When drawing, if the new layer is placed beneath or between existing layers, restate that fresh sediment settles on the current top surface.
For the tilted case, prompt: what order were these laid down in before they were bent? Discuss that we reason about the original sequence, not simply which layer is lowest on the page now.
activities.rationale: The 'read then draw' pair distinguishes a child who can label layers from one who understands the order: the draw step reveals whether they know new material is added on top. The tilted follow-up probes whether the superposition rule is understood as being about deposition order rather than a blind 'lower on the page = older'.
sourceClaims: Principle of superposition: in undisturbed sedimentary sequences the oldest layer is at the bottom and the youngest at the top; cross-sections record events in order.
learnerActions: Given a cross-section of four stacked rock layers, point to the layer laid down first and say which clue in the diagram shows it.
Explain in words how lower layers must have formed before the ones above them.
Draw where the next new layer to form would go.
Then consider a diagram where the layers are bent and tilted: decide whether the layer that was originally lowest is still the oldest, and explain your reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading the age order and knowing where new material is added are separate skills; a learner may label layers yet still read the stack top-down. New sediment is added on top, not underneath. Deformation (bending/tilting) after deposition does not change which layer was originally lowest and therefore oldest, though it can mean current depth on the page no longer matches age, so reason from the original deposition order.

activities.title: Label Earth's interior and keep it separate from strata
feedback: If a learner reasons about the crust–mantle–core diagram as if it were a deposited sequence (e.g. 'the core is oldest because it's deepest'), clarify that these layers formed by planetary processes, not by sediment settling, so superposition does not apply.
Reinforce by asking the learner to narrate what each diagram shows: 'this one shows the inside of the planet right now; that one shows the order layers were laid down over time'.
activities.rationale: Children conflate the two diagram types, so making the distinction explicit — and testing the misapplication of deeper=older to the core — protects both sub-skills. Labelling with one property per layer supports the spatial cross-section reading.
learnerActions: On a cross-section of Earth's interior, label crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core, and state one property of each.
Explicitly compare the two diagram types: Earth's interior is a spatial cross-section of the whole planet; sedimentary strata are a time record of deposited layers.
Decide whether 'deeper = older' applies to the crust–mantle–core diagram, and explain why superposition applies to deposited strata but not to Earth's internal structure.
activities.intendedInsight: Earth's interior layers (crust/mantle/core) and sedimentary strata are two different kinds of 'layers'. Superposition's deeper=older rule is about deposited sediment, not about the planet's internal structure, so it should not be applied to the core.

activities.title: Trace rock-cycle pathways as a network
feedback: If a learner treats the cycle as a single fixed order, ask them to find a second route between the same two rock types.
When a learner names the correct process for a transition (e.g. heat and pressure turning sedimentary rock to metamorphic), confirm and ask them to narrate the whole route in process terms.
activities.rationale: Tracing a pathway and seeing a rock change state as a process is applied makes the cycle read as connected pathways; asking for multiple routes directly confronts the 'fixed one-way order' misconception.
learnerActions: On a rock-cycle diagram, trace a route for a rock moving between igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic states.
Name the process that drives each transition you cross (e.g. heat and pressure, melting then cooling, weathering and erosion then deposition, compaction and cementation).
Find more than one possible pathway between two rock types to show the cycle is a network, not a single fixed one-way order.
activities.intendedInsight: Rock types can be transformed through multiple possible pathways, often through intervening stages, driven by named processes. The cycle is a network rather than one fixed sequence; this does not mean each process simply runs backward.

constraints: This is a representational skill: the objective is reading, labelling and interpreting geological diagrams, not memorising isolated facts.

Recognition-only formats that have a child name, order, or match layers can check which layers they can identify and sequence, but do not by themselves show the child can justify the order with superposition or correctly place a new layer — include a 'draw where the next layer forms' step to elicit that reasoning.

A cut-away 3D model of the planet can help convey the depth and scale of crust versus core (a spatial sub-skill); the strata/superposition reasoning is a 2D time-record and is read flat. A 3D view is an optional aid to one sub-skill, not required for the others.

Tap-to-reveal labelling supports the Earth's-interior cross-section but does not animate deposition over time; pair it with a build-the-layers activity so the superposition time-record is not left as a static picture.

Superposition's deeper=older rule applies to undisturbed, deposited sedimentary sequences; it does not apply to the crust–mantle–core structure, and bending/tilting can mean current depth no longer matches age, so reason about original deposition order.
Real roadcut/cliff photographs and a layered-jar or coloured-sand demonstration are valuable hands-on complements to any on-screen diagram.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two listed sources were not re-fetched, and both were already marked verified:false. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The two cited sources support the superposition principle and the NGSS evidence-from-patterns expectation; they do not establish comparative efficacy of any particular activity format or medium.

The NGSS claim is attached to the build-and-read activity because that activity enacts using fossils in rock layers as evidence of change over time; it underpins the overall objective and that specific fossil-evidence step, but is not evidence for any activity format being superior.

The original phrasing 'deeper fossils are older' holds only within an undisturbed sequence; it is scoped to the undisturbed stack in activity 1, and the tilted/bent follow-up in activity 2 was added so learners do not over-generalise 'lower on the page = older' to deformed strata.

The pedagogy misconception 'a cross-section shows what's on the surface' is addressed only implicitly via the cut-through interior labelling and the narration prompts; a dedicated probe could be added if desired.

probeDeeper: How does the diagram tell you which layer is older — what clue are you using?
If a river dumped new mud here next year, which layer would it become? Where would you draw it?
Here the layers are bent and tilted. Is the deepest one still the oldest? Why?
Is 'deeper is older' true for the crust–mantle–core diagram too, or only for these rock layers?
assess.correctAnswer: Points to the bottom layer as the oldest / first deposited, explaining that lower layers were laid down before the ones above them (superposition); then draws the next new layer on top of the stack.

errorPatterns.pattern: The top layer is the oldest ('it's at the top, so it came first / it's been there longest')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront it — drop coloured sand in a jar layer by layer; each new layer buries the older ones beneath.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Points to the top layer as the first-deposited / oldest.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws the next new layer at the bottom, or inserts it between existing layers
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold — new sediment settles on the current top surface; that's where the newest layer forms.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Adds new material underneath or among the existing layers rather than on top.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses Earth's-interior layers (crust/mantle/core) with sedimentary strata — applies 'deeper = older' to the core
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the two diagram types — superposition applies to deposited strata, not to Earth's internal structure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reasons about the crust–mantle–core diagram as if it were a deposited sequence.

responseLevels.gap: Can't identify the order, or reads the top layer as the oldest.
responseLevels.full: Reads deepest = oldest and justifies it (each layer deposited on top of the one before), then correctly draws the next layer on top — and distinguishes strata from the Earth-interior diagram.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies the bottom layer as oldest when prompted but can't justify it with superposition, or misplaces the new layer when drawing.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a cross-section showing four stacked rock layers. Point to the layer that was laid down first and tell me how the diagram shows it — then draw where the next new layer to form would go.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 'read then draw' pair catches a child who can label layers but reads the stack top-down (thinking the top came first because it's what you see first). The draw step then reveals whether they know new material is added on top, not underneath — separating diagram-labelling from understanding the order.
